note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

modern.note: How the letters are named in Israel today, in the general standard register. Carmit is a Hebrew voice reading Hebrew, so this system is native rather than reconstructed — but every name is written with niqqud, because unpointed Hebrew is ambiguous and six of the letter names are spelled identically to ordinary words. This register has merged ḥet with khaf, qof with kaf and ṭet with tav, and has dropped ʿayin altogether; Mizrahi and Yemenite speech keeps those distinctions, and this voice does not.

0.why: A Hebrew voice reading the Hebrew name. The pointing is doing real work: unpointed אלף is the ordinary word elef, 'a thousand', and I confirmed Carmit reads it that way — the unpointed string and the pointed אֶלֶף produce audio of identical length (0.709s), while אָלֶף is measurably different (0.649s).
0.compromise: Word-initially the aleph is a real glottal stop and that is what is heard. But in ordinary Israeli speech aleph between vowels is simply dropped, and a one-word clip cannot show that the letter's characteristic modern behaviour is disappearance.

1.why: Pointed, בֵּית is one syllable [bet]; unpointed בית is bayit, 'house'. The durations separate cleanly — 0.549s against 0.659s for בַּיִת — so the dagesh and tsere are being read.
1.compromise: Modern Israeli still keeps the bet/vet alternation, but the letter-name has the dagesh, so only the hard [b] is audible. The soft [v] that the hall's entry mentions is not demonstrated by this clip.

2.why: Native Hebrew, and gimel with dagesh is a plain [ɡ] in modern speech, which is what the name carries.
2.compromise: Modern Israeli has lost the spirantised gimel completely, so nothing here hints at the soft [ɣ] that the Sefer Yetzirah's doctrine of seven double letters presupposes. Only the Tiberian system can show that pair, and even there it shows only the hard member, since the name itself has the dagesh.

3.why: Pointed to force the letter-name and not the near-identical word: unpointed דלת is delet, 'door' — which is, appropriately enough, what the letter means. The two pointed forms differ measurably (0.688s vs 0.683s), so the qamets is read.
3.compromise: As with gimel: the soft [ð] of dalet without dagesh is gone from Modern Israeli, and this clip cannot suggest it.

4.why: Native, and unproblematic: Modern Israeli keeps [h] as a real consonant here, so the name needs no help.
4.compromise: In fast Israeli speech he is often weakened or dropped inside a phrase; in a citation form like this it is fully pronounced, which is the careful register rather than the street one.

5.why: Native. Modern vav is [v], and the name accordingly begins and ends with [v].
5.compromise: The hall transliterates this letter w, which is the classical value. Modern Hebrew has no [w] at all, so this clip is the living sound and not the historical one — that is exactly the gap the Tiberian system is here to fill.

6.why: Native, and zayin is one of the few letters whose name has been phonetically stable from the Masoretes to the present.

7.why: Native. Carmit speaks the general Israeli standard, in which ḥet is the uvular fricative [χ] — the ch of Bach that the hall's entry names.
7.compromise: This is a merger, not a preservation. In general Israeli speech ḥet is now identical to soft khaf, so this clip and the end of סָמֶךְ are the same sound. Mizrahi and Yemenite Hebrew still keep ḥet as a pharyngeal [ħ], and Carmit does not.

8.why: Native, and the honest modern value: a plain [t].
8.compromise: The hall calls this an emphatic t. There is no emphasis whatever in this clip, because there is none left in Modern Israeli — ṭet and tav are now homophones. What is heard is a merger.

9.why: Native, with holam pointed to fix the vowel.
9.compromise: Israelis very commonly say yud rather than yod, and I cannot hear which vowel Carmit produces — the pointed יוֹד and יוּד come out at identical length (0.584s), so duration cannot distinguish them. The clip may well say 'yud'. Either is current Israeli usage; the hall's spelling is the standard one.

10.compromise: The name shows only the hard member. The soft [χ] that the hall's entry mentions is heard instead at the end of סָמֶךְ, which is the one letter-name in the alphabet that ends in a spirantised khaf.

11.why: Pointed to separate the letter-name from lamad, 'he learned', which shares the consonantal skeleton exactly.
11.compromise: Duration cannot verify this one — לָמֶד and unpointed למד come out identical (0.624s), since both readings are two syllables. The pointing is trusted here on the strength of the aleph and bet tests, where it demonstrably worked.

13.why: Native, with shuruq written, so the vowel is fixed even without the pointing.

14.why: Native, pointed to separate it from samakh, 'he supported'. This name is worth attention: it ends in khaf without dagesh, so it is the alphabet's own live demonstration of begadkefat — the [χ] at its end is the soft counterpart of the [k] in כַּף.
14.compromise: As with lamed, duration cannot confirm the pointing (סָמֶךְ and סָמַךְ are both 0.738s). And the final [χ] here is now identical to ḥet, since the two have merged.

15.why: Native, and here the 'wrong' sound is the true one: general Israeli ʿayin has no consonant at all, so the name is simply [ˈajin], exactly as the hall's entry states.
15.compromise: Nothing is lost in synthesis, but a great deal has been lost in the language. The voiced pharyngeal [ʕ] survives in Mizrahi and Yemenite speech and is entirely absent here. To hear the letter's historical sound, use the Tiberian clip, which is genuinely a different consonant.

16.why: Native, pointed with dagesh for the hard [p].
16.compromise: The soft [f] is not shown by the name, since the name carries the dagesh. Modern Israeli does keep the pe/fe alternation, so this is a real live pair — just not one this clip demonstrates.

17.why: Native. Modern tsadi is the affricate [ts] the hall describes.
17.compromise: Israelis frequently call this letter tsadik rather than tsadi, by attraction to the word for 'righteous one' that the Talmudic reading in the hall's note trades on. The clip uses the standard grammarians' name.

18.compromise: The hall says qof is 'classically pronounced further back in the throat'. There is no trace of that here: Modern Israeli qof is an ordinary [k], identical to kaf. The initial consonant of this clip and of כַּף are the same sound.

19.why: Native. Modern Israeli resh is uvular, as the hall's entry says, and Carmit produces it.
19.compromise: Sephardi and older Israeli speech used an alveolar trill; the uvular is the current urban standard and the one heard here. Curiously this is the one letter where Modern Israeli may be closer to the Tiberian value than the trilled Sephardi tradition is.

20.why: Native, with the shin dot written so the [ʃ] is unambiguous.
20.compromise: The hall notes the left-dot variant sin, pronounced [s]. The name has the right dot, so only [ʃ] is heard.

21.compromise: The hall notes that the soft tav is sounded th or s in older traditions. Modern Israeli has neither — tav is always [t], and is now identical to ṭet. The soft [θ] can only be heard in the Tiberian set, where it ends four of the letter names.

tiberian.note: The pronunciation of the Tiberian Masoretes, roughly tenth-century Galilee, following Geoffrey Khan's reconstruction. It keeps what Modern Israeli has lost: ʿayin as a voiced pharyngeal, ḥet as a pharyngeal fricative distinct from khaf, ṭet emphatic against a plain tav, qof uvular against kaf, and the full begadkefat alternation — so the letter names themselves end in [f], [θ], [ð] and [χ] where the modern names end in stops. Arabic carries every letter whose value turns on a pharyngeal, an emphatic, a uvular or a spirant; Spanish carries the letters where the vowel matters more; Hebrew carries the six letters where the two traditions genuinely agree. Arabic's three-vowel system cannot render Tiberian qamets [ɔː] or segol [ɛ], and that cost is stated on every letter where it is paid.

0.why: Two things must survive and only Arabic keeps both: a genuine glottal stop at the onset — which is the entire sound value of aleph — and a final [f], because the name's pe has no dagesh. Arabic hamza is a real phonemic [ʔ]; a Spanish or Italian 'alef' would begin on a bare vowel and teach nothing.
0.compromise: The vowels are wrong. Tiberian qamets is a rounded [ɔː] and Arabic has no such vowel, so this comes out [aː]; the segol [ɛ] comes out as [a]. I also found that Maged does not lengthen alif madda — آلَف and the short أَلَف are both 0.738s — so the rate is dropped to 130 to stand in for the length.

1.why: The point of this clip is that the name ends in a spirantised tav, [θ] — a sound Modern Israeli does not possess. Castilian z is a true dental fricative [θ], word-finally and reliably (vez, pez, diez), and Spanish also gives a clean [e] and a hard initial [b]. Arabic بيث would give the [θ] but replace the vowel with [iː]; Spanish gets both right.
1.compromise: Spanish vowels are short; the rate carries the length. Nothing else of consequence — this is one of the cleanest recipes in the hall.

2.why: Spanish gui is a hard [ɡ] and the written accent forces first-syllable stress, giving [ˈɡimel] with two pure vowels. No pharyngeal or spirant is involved, so Arabic would only cost vowel quality.
2.compromise: Spanish [e] for Tiberian segol [ɛ] — one degree too close. And the name has the dagesh, so the spirantised gimel [ɣ] that makes gimel a 'double letter' is not heard in it; that sound existed in Tiberian but appears in no letter name.

3.why: Deliberately respelled with o, not a. Tiberian qamets is a rounded open-mid back vowel [ɔː], and Spanish [o] is a far better approximation to it than Arabic's unrounded [aː]. Final z gives the spirantised tav [θ], and Spanish initial d is a full stop [d].
3.compromise: Spanish [o] is close-mid where qamets is open-mid — one step too high, but much nearer than any [aː]. Segol comes out as [e] rather than [ɛ]. The soft dalet [ð] is not in this name; hear it at the end of יוֹד and לָמֶד.

4.why: Tiberian hē and Modern Israeli he are the same syllable apart from vowel length, so the Hebrew voice is simply correct and a foreign respelling would only add accent. The reduced rate supplies the length. Spanish was ruled out because Spanish h is silent.
4.compromise: Length is being simulated by slowing the whole word rather than the vowel alone.

5.why: The whole content of this clip is that Tiberian vav is [w], not [v] — the value the hall's own transliteration gives it. This string is the Arabic letter-name wāw, so Maged is reading the most native word imaginable for it, and [w] is beyond question.
5.compromise: Qamets [ɔː] is rendered as Arabic [aː]: right length, wrong quality — unrounded and lower than the target.

6.why: Tiberian and Modern agree on this name completely — [z], [a], [j], [i], [n] are all in both inventories. Sending it through Arabic or Spanish would import a foreign accent in exchange for nothing.

7.why: This is the single most important clip in the system. Arabic ح is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], a core MSA phoneme, and it is a different sound from خ [χ] — which is what Modern Israeli has turned ḥet into. Played against the [χ] that ends سَامَخْ, from the same voice, the distinction Modern Israeli lost becomes directly audible. The final ث supplies the spirantised tav [θ].
7.compromise: The vowel is wrong: Arabic has no [eː], so tsere comes out as [iː]. Both consonants are exact; the vowel is the price.

8.why: Arabic ط is a genuinely pharyngealised [tˤ] — the emphatic the hall's entry names and Modern Israeli no longer has. Set against تَاو for tav, from the same voice, this is a real minimal contrast rather than an assertion.
8.compromise: Tsere comes out as Arabic [iː] rather than [eː]. Arabic emphasis also colours the following vowel backward, which Tiberian emphasis may or may not have done to the same degree — this is Arabic emphasis standing in for Hebrew emphasis, not a reconstruction of it.

9.why: The name ends in a dalet without dagesh, so Tiberian gives [ð]. Arabic ذ is an unambiguous voiced dental fricative in any position, including finally.
9.compromise: My weakest recipe in this system. Arabic has no [oː], so holam comes out [uː] and the clip is closer to 'yoodh' than to [joːð]. Spanish 'iod' would fix the vowel, but Castilian word-final -d is unstable — frequently devoiced to [θ] or dropped entirely — which would destroy the one consonant this clip exists to demonstrate. I took the wrong vowel over the unreliable consonant.

10.why: This string is Arabic's own letter-name kāf. Its value is that it comes from the same voice as قُوفْ, so the kaf/qof distinction — velar [k] against uvular [q] — is heard as a contrast between two clips rather than described. The final ف gives the spirantised pe [f], since the name's pe has no dagesh.
10.compromise: Qamets [ɔː] becomes Arabic [aː], unrounded and lower.

11.why: The final ذ is the spirantised dalet [ð], which is the point of the clip and which Modern Israeli has entirely lost. Arabic delivers it word-finally without hedging.
11.compromise: Both vowels are wrong: qamets [ɔː] comes out [aː], and segol [ɛ] comes out [a], so the two syllables sound more alike than they should. Spanish 'lómed' would give better vowels but risks the same final-d collapse described under yod, which would turn the [ð] into [θ] and confuse lamed with dalet.

12.why: Identical in both traditions but for length; the Hebrew voice is simply right, and the reduced rate carries the long tsere.
12.compromise: Length simulated by slowing the word rather than the vowel.

13.why: Same reasoning as mem: nothing in this name has changed except vowel length, so Hebrew carries it and the rate supplies the shuruq's length.

14.why: Arabic is chosen over Hebrew here specifically so that the final [χ] of خ comes from the same throat as the [ħ] of حِيثْ. That is what makes the ḥet/khaf distinction demonstrable: two clips, one voice, two clearly different fricatives. Arabic س is a plain [s], correctly non-emphatic against ṣadi.
14.compromise: Qamets becomes [aː] and segol becomes [a]. Arabic خ is post-velar to uvular, which is the right region for Tiberian soft khaf, though the exact Tiberian articulation is not recoverable to that precision.

15.why: Arabic ع is a voiced pharyngeal — the same consonant Tiberian ʿayin was, and one that no European voice can even gesture at. Compare with the modern clip, where the letter has no consonant at all: this is the sharpest before-and-after in the hall.
15.compromise: The vowels are short [a] and [i] in both traditions, so they are essentially right; only the Arabic voice quality is foreign. Note that this is Arabic's ʿayin doing duty for Hebrew's, on the historical grounds that the two are cognate — not an independent reconstruction of the Tiberian articulation.

16.why: Arabic is impossible here — Modern Standard Arabic has no [p] whatever, and Maged would substitute [b] or [f], which would make pe indistinguishable from bet. Spanish gives an unaspirated [p] and a pure [e]; 'pe' is literally the Spanish name of the letter P, so it is a real word rather than a guess.
16.compromise: Spanish [e] is short; the rate carries the length. English 'pay' was rejected because English aspirates initial p and diphthongises the vowel.

17.why: Two lost consonants in one word. Arabic ص is a pharyngealised [sˤ], which is what Tiberian ṣadi was — an emphatic sibilant, not the affricate [ts] Modern Israeli says; and ذ gives the spirantised dalet [ð]. Arabic delivers both natively and the final [iː] is correct as written.
17.compromise: Qamets becomes [aː]. And the name itself is contested: the older Tiberian form is ṣāḏē, with [eː], which Arabic cannot produce; I have used the equally attested ṣāḏî so that the clip matches the pronunciation stated above it rather than quietly missing it.

18.why: Arabic ق is a voiceless uvular stop [q] — the hall's 'further back in the throat', produced natively rather than approximated. Against كَاف from the same voice, the kaf/qof merger that Modern Israeli has undergone can be heard being undone. The final ف is the spirantised pe [f].
18.compromise: Holam [oː] comes out as Arabic [uː], since Arabic has no mid back vowel. The consonants are exact; the vowel is not.

19.why: Khan reconstructs the default Tiberian resh as uvular, and Modern Israeli resh is uvular — so on this one letter the living pronunciation is arguably closer to the Masoretes than the Sephardi trill is, and Carmit can simply say it.
19.compromise: The uvular reconstruction of Tiberian resh is an argued position, not a settled fact, and Tiberian also had a second, alveolar allophone of resh in specific consonantal environments which no single clip can show. Vowel length is supplied by rate.

20.why: Unchanged between the traditions apart from length; the Hebrew voice needs no assistance and the shin dot is written.
20.compromise: Length simulated by rate. As in the modern set, the left-dot variant sin [s] is not demonstrated by the name.

21.why: Two jobs. Arabic ت is a plain unaspirated dental [t], which set against طِيثْ makes the ṭet/tav contrast audible from one voice; and the final و is [w], the classical value of vav that Modern Israeli has replaced with [v].
21.compromise: Qamets [ɔː] becomes Arabic [aː]. The name has the dagesh, so this clip shows only the hard tav — the soft [θ] is heard instead at the end of bēṯ, dāleṯ, ḥēṯ and ṭēṯ.
